claims.claim: NIST's 2017 SP 800-63B reversal says verifiers should not impose composition rules (character-class mixes) and should not require periodic password changes.
claims.episode_span: In 2017 NIST released SP 800-63-3, which removed mandatory character-class rules and eliminated forced periodic changes for most accounts
claims.source_title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines - Authentication and Lifecycle Management
claims.supporting_quote: Verifiers SHOULD NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types or prohibiting consecutively repeated characters) for memorized secrets. Verifiers SHOULD NOT require memorized secrets to be changed arbitrarily (e.g., periodically).

claims.claim: The 2017 guidance instead recommends long, memorable passphrases (allowing at least 64 characters, any characters including spaces).
claims.episode_span: instead recommending long passphrases that users could remember
claims.source_title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines - Authentication and Lifecycle Management
claims.supporting_quote: Allow at least 64 characters in length to support the use of passphrases. Encourage users to make memorized secrets as lengthy as they want, using any characters they like (including spaces), thus aiding memorization.

claims.claim: Under composition rules, users converge on a small set of predictable strategies (e.g. 'password' becomes 'Password1').
claims.episode_span: most people converged on a small set of strategies
claims.source_title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines - Authentication and Lifecycle Management
claims.supporting_quote: Research has shown, however, that users respond in very predictable ways to the requirements imposed by composition rules

claims.claim: Analyses of breached password databases show composition rules delivered much less security benefit than expected, at severe usability cost.
claims.episode_span: so the theoretical entropy advantage disappeared in practice
claims.source_title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines - Authentication and Lifecycle Management
claims.supporting_quote: analyses of breached password databases reveal that the benefit of such rules is not nearly as significant as initially thought

claims.claim: In 2003 NIST's Bill Burr drafted the password guidance (NIST SP 800-63 Appendix A) that spread the complexity-and-rotation rules.
claims.episode_span: In the spring of 2003 a mid-level NIST engineer named William Burr finished
claims.source_title: The Guy Who Invented Those Annoying Password Rules Now Regrets Wasting Your Time - Gizmodo
claims.supporting_quote: In 2003, Burr drafted an eight-page guide on how to create secure passwords

claims.claim: Burr, retired, told the Wall Street Journal in 2017 that he regretted his earlier password advice.
claims.episode_span: William Burr, by then retired, told the Wall Street Journal that he regretted the earlier advice
claims.source_title: The Guy Who Invented Those Annoying Password Rules Now Regrets Wasting Your Time - Gizmodo
claims.supporting_quote: Bill Burr told The Wall Street Journal recently, admitting that his research into passwords mostly came from a white paper written in the 1980s

claims.claim: Burr's rules required numbers and special characters plus changes every three months, and became near-universal policy.
claims.episode_span: require passwords with uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and at least one special character, plus a forced change every ninety days
claims.source_title: Man who made passwords hard to remember regrets rules that 'drive people crazy' - CBC Radio
claims.supporting_quote: About 15 years ago, Burr wrote information security guidelines for the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology. His section on passwords included instructions to fill them with numbers and characters and change them every three months.
